title: The Ultimate Capsule Wardrobe Guide: How Many Clothes Do You Really Need?
excerpt: A wardrobe full of clothes doesn't necessarily mean you have more outfits. Here's how many pieces you actually need — and how to build a wardrobe that works as a system, not a pile.
content:
A wardrobe full of clothes doesn't necessarily mean you have more outfits. Sometimes, the opposite happens. You open your wardrobe and think, “I have nothing to wear.” The problem isn't always a lack of clothes. It's often a lack of versatile pieces that work together. That's where a capsule wardrobe comes in.

A capsule wardrobe is a thoughtfully curated collection of clothes, shoes and accessories that can be mixed and matched to create a large number of outfits without owning an overwhelming number of pieces. There is no universal magic number. Your lifestyle, climate, profession, personal style and laundry routine all matter. However, a good starting point is around 30–40 core clothing pieces, excluding underwear, sleepwear, workout clothes and occasion-specific pieces.

What Is a Capsule Wardrobe?

Instead of buying individual clothes because you like them, you build your wardrobe around versatile basics, a consistent colour palette, pieces that can be layered, clothes that suit your lifestyle, a few statement pieces, and shoes and accessories that work across multiple outfits.

The goal isn't to own as little as possible. The goal is to make more outfits from fewer, better-connected pieces. Think of your wardrobe as a system rather than a collection.

How Many Pieces Should Be in a Women's Capsule Wardrobe?

For most women, a practical starting point is around 35–45 core clothing pieces. Someone working from home may need fewer formal clothes; someone in an office may need more shirts, trousers and structured layers. Someone in a warm climate may need very little knitwear, while someone in a colder climate may need considerably more.

  • T-shirts & basic tops — 5–7
  • Shirts & blouses — 4–5
  • Trousers & jeans — 4–6
  • Skirts — 1–2
  • Dresses — 2–4
  • Jackets & outerwear — 3–4
  • Knitwear — 2–3
  • Occasion pieces — 2–3

A simple rule: try building your wardrobe around 70% versatile basics + 20% personality pieces + 10% statement pieces — white/black/neutral tops, straight-leg jeans, tailored trousers, a versatile blazer, a neutral dress, a few layering pieces, one or two colourful or printed pieces, and your favourite statement accessories. The basics create the foundation; the personality pieces make the wardrobe feel like you.

How Many Pieces Should Be in a Men's Capsule Wardrobe?

Men can generally start with around 30–40 core clothing pieces, excluding underwear, gym wear, sleepwear and specialised clothing.

  • T-shirts — 5–7
  • Casual shirts — 3–5
  • Formal shirts — 3–5
  • Jeans & casual trousers — 4–5
  • Formal trousers — 2–3
  • Shorts — 2–3
  • Sweaters/overshirts — 2–3
  • Jackets/blazers — 2–3

Again, these numbers are a starting point, not a rule. A corporate professional may need significantly more formalwear; a creative professional may need more casual and statement pieces. Your capsule wardrobe should reflect your actual life, not someone else's Pinterest board.

The 5-4-3-2-1 Capsule Wardrobe Formula

If you're starting from scratch, try the 5-4-3-2-1 method. The formula is deliberately simple — once you have this foundation, you can expand based on your lifestyle.

  • 5 Tops — 2 everyday basics, 1 elevated top, 1 shirt, 1 statement piece
  • 4 Bottoms — 1 pair of jeans, 1 tailored trouser, 1 casual trouser, 1 seasonal or statement bottom
  • 3 Layers — blazer, jacket, cardigan/overshirt
  • 2 Shoes — start with two highly versatile pairs, like sneakers and loafers/boots/flats
  • 1 Statement Piece — a colourful jacket, printed dress, statement shirt, bold shoes or statement jewellery

Your Capsule Wardrobe Should Start With Your Lifestyle

Before buying anything, ask yourself: what do I actually do every week?

  • If you work in an office five days a week, your wardrobe should prioritise workwear.
  • If you're remote, you might need more elevated casualwear.
  • If you travel frequently, prioritise wrinkle-resistant, versatile pieces.
  • If you attend lots of events, add occasionwear.
  • If you live somewhere hot and humid, breathable fabrics should make up a larger part of your wardrobe.

Your wardrobe should serve your life — not the other way around.

Start With Your Core Colours

One of the easiest ways to make a capsule wardrobe work is to create a simple colour palette. Start with 2–4 neutral colours — Classic (Black + White + Grey + Navy), Warm (Cream + Beige + Brown + Olive), Soft (White + Taupe + Blush + Denim) or Dark (Black + Charcoal + Navy + Burgundy) — then add 1–3 accent colours.

This makes it much easier to mix and match. A navy trouser, for example, can work with a white shirt, beige sweater, blue shirt, grey T-shirt or burgundy knit. One piece can create multiple outfits because the colours already work together.

The One-to-Three Rule

Before adding a new item to your capsule wardrobe, ask: can I style this piece in at least three different ways? For example, before buying a new blazer, can you wear it with:

  • Jeans + T-shirt
  • Tailored trousers + shirt
  • Dress + heels/sneakers

If yes, it earns its place. If you can only imagine wearing it with one outfit, pause before buying. This simple rule can dramatically reduce impulse purchases.

How to Build Your Capsule Wardrobe Step by Step

  • Step 1: Empty your wardrobe. Take everything out and put it somewhere you can see it, then sort into Keep → Maybe → Remove.
  • Step 2: Identify your most-worn pieces. Look at what you actually wear, not what you wish you wore — your most-worn pieces reveal your real personal style.
  • Step 3: Find your wardrobe gaps. You might have 8 tops, 7 dresses and 0 versatile trousers — the problem usually isn't that you need more clothes, it's that you need balance.
  • Step 4: Build your basics first — the pieces you'll wear repeatedly, like a white top, tailored trousers and versatile shoes.
  • Step 5: Add personality — colour, prints, interesting silhouettes, textures, statement jewellery, bags, shoes and jackets. Minimal doesn't have to mean boring.

How Many Outfits Can a Capsule Wardrobe Create?

Imagine you have 5 tops × 4 bottoms = 20 combinations. Add 3 layers and 2 pairs of shoes, and the number of possible combinations grows dramatically. But not every mathematical combination will make a good outfit — the goal isn't simply to maximise the number of combinations, it's to create high-quality combinations that actually suit you. A well-designed capsule wardrobe can give you dozens of everyday outfits from a surprisingly small number of pieces.

Don't Forget Accessories

Accessories can completely change an outfit without adding many clothes to your wardrobe — especially useful if you prefer a smaller clothing collection but still want variety.

  • For women — everyday earrings, statement earrings, necklace, watch, belt, everyday bag, occasion bag, sunglasses
  • For men — watch, belt, sunglasses, cap, tie, pocket square, everyday bag

When Should You Add Something New?

Don't automatically add new clothes every time you feel bored with your wardrobe. Instead, ask:

  • Does it fill a gap?
  • Does it work with what I already own?
  • Can I create at least three outfits with it?
  • Will I realistically wear it?
  • Does it fit my current lifestyle?
  • Do I already own something similar?

If the answer is mostly yes, it may be a useful addition. If not, save your money.

The Capsule Wardrobe Isn't a Number

The biggest misconception about capsule wardrobes is that everyone needs exactly 30, 40 or 50 pieces. You don't. A capsule wardrobe for a minimalist living in a warm city could look completely different from the wardrobe of a lawyer living in a cold climate.

The right number is the number that allows you to get dressed easily, feel good in what you wear, have enough variety, and avoid unnecessary clutter.

Your wardrobe should make your mornings easier — not become another thing to manage.

Turn Your Wardrobe Into a System With AHVI

Your wardrobe already contains a lot of information — what you wear frequently, what colours you prefer, what pieces you never reach for, what outfits you repeat, what categories you're missing. But most of us don't have that information organised. That's where AHVI comes in: digitise your wardrobe and let AHVI understand what you own, so you can interact with your digital wardrobe, discover combinations and get styled around what you already own. Your wardrobe becomes searchable, organised and easier to use — because the goal isn't to own the perfect wardrobe, it's to get more out of the wardrobe you already have.

Your Capsule Wardrobe Checklist

  • Women — 5–7 everyday tops, 4–5 shirts/blouses, 4–6 bottoms, 2–4 dresses, 2–3 knitwear pieces, 3–4 jackets/layers, 2–4 pairs of versatile shoes, everyday + statement accessories
  • Men — 5–7 T-shirts, 3–5 casual shirts, 3–5 formal shirts, 4–5 trousers/jeans, 2–3 shorts, 2–3 layers, 2–3 jackets/blazers, 2–4 pairs of versatile shoes, everyday accessories

Start with what you need. Add what you love. Remove what you don't wear. That's the essence of a capsule wardrobe.

title: Colour Analysis: How to Find the Colours That Actually Suit You
excerpt: Personal colour analysis helps you understand which colours tend to complement your natural colouring — from undertones and colour seasons to building a working palette.
content:
Have you ever worn a colour that made you look instantly fresh? And then worn another one that somehow made you look tired — even though you loved the outfit? It might not be the clothes. It might be the colour.

Personal colour analysis helps you understand which colours tend to complement your natural colouring, making it easier to choose clothes, jewellery, makeup and even hair colours. You don't have to stop wearing colours you love — the idea is simply to understand which shades work with you, rather than constantly guessing.

What Is Colour Analysis?

Colour analysis is a way of identifying colours that harmonise with your natural colouring. It usually considers skin undertone, skin depth, hair colour, eye colour and the overall contrast between your features. The result is often a personal colour palette containing shades that are likely to complement you. You may hear terms such as Warm, Cool, Neutral, Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter — different ways of organising colour characteristics.

Step 1: Understand Your Skin Undertone

Your skin tone and undertone are not the same thing. Your skin tone describes how light or deep your skin appears. Your undertone describes the subtle colour underneath your skin.

  • Warm — golden, peachy or yellow characteristics. Try cream, camel, terracotta, coral, mustard, olive, warm brown, gold.
  • Cool — pink, red or bluish characteristics. Try true white, navy, cobalt, berry, cool pink, emerald, lavender, silver.
  • Neutral — sits between warm and cool, making it easier to wear a broader range of colours. Both gold and silver jewellery may work well, and both warm and cool shades can complement you.

How Can You Find Your Undertone?

  • Look at your veins in natural daylight — green leans warm, blue/purple leans cool, a mix or difficult to determine suggests neutral. This is only a quick indication; lighting and skin depth can affect how your veins appear.
  • Try gold and silver jewellery near your face — notice which one makes your complexion appear more balanced. If both work, you may be neutral, and if you love both, you don't have to choose.
  • Try white vs cream — hold a bright white and a soft cream fabric near your face. Bright white looking more flattering leans cool, cream feeling more harmonious leans warm, and both looking good suggests neutral.

What Are Colour Seasons?

One of the most popular approaches to colour analysis divides people into four seasonal families:

  • Spring — warm, light and bright: peach, coral, warm pink, light green, turquoise, cream, golden yellow.
  • Summer — cool, soft and muted: dusty rose, powder blue, lavender, soft grey, mauve, cool pink.
  • Autumn — warm, deep and earthy: rust, olive, camel, chocolate brown, mustard, burnt orange, deep teal.
  • Winter — cool, deep and high-contrast: black, bright white, cobalt, emerald, burgundy, fuchsia, icy pink.

These categories can be further divided into more specific sub-seasons, such as Soft Autumn, Deep Winter or Bright Spring. Remember: seasonal colour analysis is a framework, not a rulebook. Your colouring can sit between categories, and personal preference still matters.

Your Best Colours Aren't Just About Your Skin

One common mistake is choosing colours based only on skin undertone. Colour harmony can also depend on your hair — your natural hair colour contributes to your overall colouring and contrast — and your eyes, since eye colour can help explain why certain shades make your eyes appear more noticeable.

Consider the contrast between your skin, hair and eyes too. Someone with very dark hair and light skin may have higher contrast than someone whose hair, eyes and skin are closer in depth — this can influence whether stronger or softer colour combinations feel more harmonious.

How to Use Colour Analysis in Your Wardrobe

Knowing your palette is useful. Knowing how to use it is even more useful. You don't need to replace your entire wardrobe — start with the pieces you wear closest to your face: tops, shirts, dresses, jackets, scarves, jewellery.

If a colour isn't particularly flattering near your face, you can still wear it — just move it further away. Instead of a colour you don't love as a top, try it as trousers, a skirt, shoes, a bag or a belt. This lets you enjoy more colours without letting them dominate your look.

Build Your Wardrobe Around Three Colour Groups

Once you understand your palette, divide your wardrobe colours into three groups.

  • Your neutrals — black, white, cream, beige, navy, grey, brown. These form the foundation of your wardrobe — choose the ones that work best with your colouring; you don't necessarily need every one.
  • Your best colours — the shades that consistently make you feel great and can become your wardrobe's signature colours, e.g. olive + cream + chocolate brown, or navy + white + berry, or camel + rust + ivory.
  • Your statement colours — bright red, fuchsia, cobalt, orange, emerald, lavender. You don't need many — a few statement pieces can completely change a neutral wardrobe.

What About Jewellery?

Colour analysis isn't just for clothes — it can also help when choosing jewellery. If warmer metals complement your colouring, consider yellow gold, gold vermeil, bronze and warm-toned metals. If cooler metals complement your colouring, consider silver, platinum and white-toned metals. If you're neutral, you may be able to move between both. Don't forget gemstones — your personal palette can help you choose stones that complement your clothing and natural colouring.

Colour Analysis for Men

Colour analysis isn't just a women's styling tool — it can be particularly useful for building a men's capsule wardrobe. Start with versatile basics (T-shirts, shirts, trousers, jeans, blazers, jackets, shoes), then identify the colours that work best together.

A man with warm colouring might build around cream + olive + camel + brown + navy. Someone with cooler colouring might prefer white + charcoal + navy + burgundy + cobalt. The result is a wardrobe where more pieces naturally work together.

Don't Throw Away Everything That Isn't in Your Palette

This is important: colour analysis should make getting dressed easier, not create another set of rules. You can wear whatever you want. If you love neon green and it isn't considered part of your palette, wear it. If black isn't technically your "best" colour but you love black, keep wearing it.

Instead of asking ‘Am I allowed to wear this?’, ask ‘How can I style this so I feel great in it?’

You can balance a difficult colour with another shade, use it away from your face, or introduce it through accessories. Personal style always comes first.

How to Build a Personal Colour Palette

You don't need 50 colours. Start with around 4–6 neutrals, 5–8 everyday colours and 3–5 statement colours — enough variety without making your wardrobe complicated. Once you have your palette, shopping becomes easier: instead of asking “Do I like this top?”, you can ask “Does this top work with the wardrobe I already have?” That's a much better question.

Colour Analysis + Capsule Wardrobe = A More Useful Wardrobe

This is where colour analysis becomes particularly powerful. Imagine your wardrobe contains 5 tops, 4 bottoms, 3 layers and 3 pairs of shoes — that's already enough for many combinations. Now imagine those pieces also share a complementary colour palette. Your wardrobe becomes significantly easier to mix and match — instead of owning individual outfits, you're building a connected wardrobe system.

Let AHVI Find Your Colours

Understanding your colours is useful. Remembering all of it every time you shop or get dressed? That's where technology can help. AHVI is designed to understand more than just the clothes in your wardrobe — with AHVI Lens and Face Scan, your personal styling experience can take into account your colouring, wardrobe and preferences.

You can digitise your wardrobe, understand your colour palette and use that information when discovering outfits. Instead of asking “What colour should I wear?”, you can start with “What works for me — and what can I create with what I already own?” That's the difference between simply having a wardrobe and actually understanding it.

Your Quick Colour Analysis Checklist

  • Identify your skin tone, explore your undertone, and compare gold vs silver and white vs cream.
  • Consider your hair and eye colour, and understand your overall contrast.
  • Identify your strongest neutrals, choose 5–8 colours you love, and add a few statement colours.
  • Use accessories to experiment — and don't throw away colours you love.
  • Build your wardrobe around colours that work together.

Colour analysis isn't about restricting your wardrobe. It's about understanding colour well enough to make better choices. Your best palette isn't a box. It's a starting point for discovering your style.

title: Body Shape Guide: Understanding Your Shape & Dressing With Confidence
excerpt: Understanding your body shape can help you recognise how different cuts, proportions and layers interact with your natural proportions — for both men and women.
content:
Have you ever tried on an outfit that looked amazing on someone else — but somehow didn't feel the same on you? It may not be the outfit. It may be the silhouette. And no, this isn't about changing your body. It's about understanding what you already have and using clothing to create the look and proportions you want.

Your body shape can also change over time — weight distribution, muscle, age, pregnancy and lifestyle can all affect proportions. So think of body shape as a styling framework, not a permanent label.

How Body Shape Works

Body-shape systems generally look at the relationship between shoulders, bust/chest, waist, hips and overall silhouette. Two people can wear the same size and have completely different proportions — that's why knowing your measurements isn't always enough. The goal is to understand your proportions, then experiment with clothing accordingly.

Men's Body Shapes

Five useful styling categories: Inverted Triangle, Trapezoid, Rectangle, Triangle, Oval.

  • Inverted Triangle — shoulders and chest noticeably broader than waist and hips. The goal isn't to hide broad shoulders, it's to balance the silhouette: straight-leg or relaxed trousers, structured-but-not-exaggerated jackets, minimal shoulder padding. Be mindful of extremely padded shoulders or very tight, tapered trousers.
  • Trapezoid — shoulders slightly wider than the waist, a naturally balanced silhouette. Focus on a clean, intentional look: tailored shirts, straight-leg trousers, chinos, blazers, polos, crew-neck tees, classic denim. A versatile shape for experimenting with different aesthetics.
  • Rectangle — shoulders, waist and hips relatively similar in width. Create definition with structured jackets, layering, overshirts, bomber jackets, horizontal details, tapered trousers and belts — a structured jacket over a simple T-shirt adds visual shape.
  • Triangle — waist and lower body appear broader than the shoulders. Add structure to the upper body (jackets, overshirts, horizontal stripes, layering, brighter or more detailed tops) while keeping the lower half streamlined with straight-leg, darker trousers.
  • Oval — the midsection is the most prominent area, with shoulders and legs appearing relatively narrower. Aim for comfortable, clean vertical lines: relaxed but structured clothing, straight-leg trousers, open overshirts, vertical layers, monochromatic outfits, well-fitted jackets.

Women's Body Shapes

Five commonly used categories: Apple, Pear, Hourglass, Inverted Triangle, Rectangle.

  • Apple — the midsection is often the most prominent part of the silhouette. Create comfortable definition and flow with V-neck tops, wrap-style silhouettes, open jackets, straight-leg trousers, A-line skirts, long vertical layers and monochromatic outfits — an open blazer or long cardigan can create a visually elongated silhouette.
  • Pear — hips wider than the shoulders, more visual weight through the lower body. Bring attention toward the upper body while keeping the lower half streamlined: structured shoulders, interesting necklines, statement earrings, cropped jackets, bright or detailed tops, darker lower-half colours.
  • Hourglass — shoulders/bust and hips relatively balanced, with a noticeably defined waist. Use pieces that acknowledge the waist — wrap dresses, fitted blazers, high-waisted trousers, waist-defined dresses, belted outfits. Definition, not tightness, is what matters.
  • Inverted Triangle — shoulders or bust broader than the hips. Add visual weight to the lower half while keeping the upper body cleaner: wide-leg trousers, A-line skirts, flared trousers, full skirts, detailed bottoms, simple necklines, minimal shoulder structure.
  • Rectangle — shoulders, waist and hips relatively similar in width, creating a straighter silhouette. Either embrace the clean, straight line or create definition around the waist with tailored blazers, cropped jackets, belted outfits, high-waisted trousers and layering. A rectangle shape doesn't need to fake curves — straight, minimalist silhouettes can look incredibly polished here.

How to Find Your Body Shape

You don't need to rely entirely on a mirror. Take a full-length photo or measure around the fullest part of your shoulders, the fullest part of your bust/chest, the narrowest part of your waist, and the fullest part of your hips — then compare the proportions rather than focusing on the absolute numbers. Measurements are a guide; your visual proportions and how clothes sit on your body matter too.

What If You Don't Fit One Shape?

You might not — body-shape categories are simplified systems. You may have characteristics of more than one shape, and your proportions can change over time. Instead of asking “What body shape am I?”, try asking “What are my proportions, and what silhouettes do I enjoy?” That's much more useful for personal styling.

Body Shape Isn't the Same as Body Size

This is important: body shape describes proportions, not size. You can have an hourglass shape at many different sizes, or a rectangle shape at many different sizes. You can be petite, tall, plus-size, muscular or slim and still fall into any of these shape categories.

There is no ‘ideal’ body shape. There is only your body and how you want to style it.

The Best Fit Is the One That Makes You Feel Good

Body-shape guides often tell you what to avoid. We think it's more useful to focus on what you can experiment with. Want to wear oversized clothes? Do it. Love skinny jeans? Wear them. Want to emphasise your shoulders, or highlight your hips? Go for it. Styling isn't about following rules — it's about understanding proportions well enough to make intentional choices.

Body Shape + Colour + Wardrobe = Personal Styling

Body shape is only one part of personal style. Your best outfits can come from combining body proportions, colour palette, personal style, lifestyle, occasion, weather and what you already own. A blazer isn't simply a blazer — it's a blazer in your colour, on your body, styled with your wardrobe, for your occasion.

Let AHVI Understand Your Style

Knowing your body shape is useful. Knowing how it interacts with your entire wardrobe is even more useful. AHVI can bring together the information that normally lives in your head — what you own, what colours work for you, what silhouettes you prefer, where you're going and what the occasion is.

Digitise your wardrobe and interact with AHVI to discover outfits built around you. Because personal styling shouldn't be “Here are the clothes you should wear” — it should be “Here's what you have. Here's what works. Let's create something you love.”

Your Body Is Not a Problem to Solve

A body-shape guide should never make you feel like your body needs correcting. Use these categories as a styling language: learn your proportions, experiment with silhouettes, understand what makes you feel confident — and then wear whatever makes you feel like yourself.

Your shape is information — not a limitation.

title: Your Style Persona: Why What You Wear Depends on Your Mood
excerpt: One day, oversized blazer and clean trousers. The next, sequins for Friday night. Meet the 6 AHVI style personas and why your wardrobe can hold all of them.
content:
Who says you have just one style? One day, you might want to wear an oversized blazer, clean trousers and barely-there jewellery. The next day, a flowy dress, handcrafted accessories and earthy textures. And then Friday night arrives — and suddenly, you're looking for sequins. That's not inconsistent style. That's personal style.

Your style can change with your mood, your plans, your environment and even the version of yourself you want to feel like that day. At AHVI, we think of these different expressions as style personas.

What Is a Style Persona?

A style persona is a way of describing the visual language you naturally gravitate towards. It can influence the clothes you choose, your colours, silhouettes, fabrics, jewellery, shoes, accessories, hair and beauty — even the way you put an outfit together.

But here's the important part: you don't have to be just one persona. You can be minimal on Monday, bohemian on Saturday and glamorous that night. Your style persona can shift with how you feel and what you want to express.

Your Style Is More Like a Playlist Than a Label

Think about your music taste — you probably don't listen to the same song every day. Your playlist changes depending on whether you're working, travelling, exercising, going on a date or having a quiet Sunday. Your wardrobe can work the same way, with different style moods for different moments.

Want to feel powerful? You might reach for tailoring. Want to feel relaxed? Soft fabrics and easy silhouettes. Want to feel adventurous? Colour, texture or accessories. Your wardrobe isn't just about how you look — it's also about how you want to feel.

The 6 AHVI Style Personas

AHVI uses six core style personas to help understand different expressions of personal style. Let's meet them.

  • Clean Minimalist — calm, effortless, intentional; the days you don't want your outfit to try too hard. Clean lines, neutral colours (white, black, cream, beige, grey, navy), simple silhouettes, quality basics, minimal accessories. Staples: crisp white shirt, tailored trousers, straight-leg jeans, minimal blazer, simple knitwear, structured handbag, sleek sneakers, delicate jewellery. The feeling: “I have my life together.”
  • Boho Artisanal — free, creative, earthy, individual; about texture and craftsmanship rather than looking perfectly coordinated. Handcrafted details, natural fabrics, embroidery, layering (terracotta, olive, rust, mustard, cream, brown, deep teal). Staples: flowy dresses, relaxed trousers, embroidered tops, textured layers, handcrafted jewellery, artisanal bags, printed scarves, earth-toned footwear. The feeling: “I found this somewhere amazing.”
  • Street Cool — confident, relaxed, unbothered; about attitude, mixing casual pieces with unexpected proportions and layers. Oversized silhouettes, denim, sneakers, cargo trousers, statement accessories (black, charcoal, white, denim, olive, burgundy, with occasional pops of colour). Staples: oversized T-shirt, baggy or straight denim, cargo trousers, bomber jacket, sneakers, baseball cap, crossbody bag, statement sunglasses. The feeling: “I didn't overthink this.”
  • Soft Elegant — feminine, romantic, refined, effortless; gentle silhouettes, beautiful fabrics and subtle details. Fluid silhouettes, soft fabrics, delicate details, draping (blush, ivory, champagne, dusty rose, powder blue, soft beige). Staples: midi dress, soft blouse, tailored trousers, fine knitwear, delicate jewellery, elegant flats, small handbag, light layers. The feeling: “Everything feels a little softer today.”
  • Party Glam — bold, playful, magnetic; for the days when blending in isn't the objective. Sequins, metallics, satin, rhinestones, bold silhouettes, statement jewellery, heels (black, silver, gold, ruby, emerald, fuchsia). Staples: statement dress, satin top, metallic skirt, statement earrings, heels, rhinestone accessories, mini bag, bold makeup. The feeling: “Tonight is an event.”
  • Formal Chic — powerful, polished, sophisticated; sharp tailoring, refined details and pieces that communicate confidence. Tailoring, structured silhouettes, crisp fabrics, classic accessories, polished shoes, refined jewellery (black, navy, charcoal, white, camel, burgundy). Staples: tailored blazer, trousers, crisp shirt, structured dress, loafers or pumps, classic watch, structured bag, minimal jewellery. The feeling: “I'm here for business — and I came prepared.”

You Can Be More Than One Persona

This is where personal style gets interesting — you don't have to choose one. You might be 70% Clean Minimalist, 20% Soft Elegant, 10% Party Glam. Or 50% Street Cool, 30% Clean Minimalist, 20% Boho Artisanal. Your style can be a combination of different personas — in fact, your most interesting outfits often happen between two aesthetics.

Style Blending Creates Your Signature

  • Clean Minimalist + Street Cool — tailored trousers + oversized T-shirt + sneakers + structured bag.
  • Boho Artisanal + Soft Elegant — flowy dress + delicate jewellery + handcrafted bag.
  • Formal Chic + Street Cool — tailored blazer + relaxed denim + sneakers.
  • Clean Minimalist + Party Glam — black column dress + minimal jewellery + statement metallic bag.
  • Soft Elegant + Party Glam — satin dress + delicate heels + dramatic earrings.

You don't have to dress according to a single aesthetic. You can create your own.

Your Mood Can Change Your Style

When you want to feel productive, you might naturally reach for Formal Chic or Clean Minimalist. When you want to feel comfortable, Street Cool or Soft Elegant. When you want to feel creative, Boho Artisanal. When you want to feel confident and powerful, Formal Chic. When you want attention, Party Glam. When you want to disappear into the day, Clean Minimalist. There isn't one correct answer — your wardrobe can respond to your emotional state instead of fighting it.

Your Style Persona Can Change With the Occasion

Mood isn't the only factor — your environment matters too. Imagine you have a dinner at 8 PM: AHVI might need to understand where you're going, who you're meeting, the weather, how formal the occasion is, how you feel today, and what you already own. The same person could receive completely different outfit recommendations depending on the answers — and that's what makes personal styling actually personal.

How to Discover Your Style Persona

You don't need a complicated quiz. Start by looking at your wardrobe for patterns — which colours keep appearing, which silhouettes you buy repeatedly, whether you prefer structured or relaxed, neutral or colourful, minimal or detailed, classic or experimental, soft or sharp, understated or dramatic. Your answers start revealing your style personas.

Try the Three-Word Style Test

Look at your favourite outfits and describe each one using three words — e.g. Clean · Modern · Effortless, or Feminine · Soft · Romantic, or Bold · Relaxed · Cool. Do this with 5–10 outfits, then look for recurring words. Those patterns are clues to your personal style.

Your Wardrobe Doesn't Need to Match One Aesthetic

This is one of the biggest mistakes people make when trying to “find their style.” They decide “I'm a minimalist” and stop themselves from wearing anything colourful, or “I'm a boho girl” and feel like they can't wear a structured blazer. But your personality isn't one-dimensional — why should your wardrobe be?

You can have a neutral capsule wardrobe and still have a dramatic evening persona. You can love streetwear and still dress formally for work.

You can be minimalist during the week and completely glamorous on Saturday night. Your style can evolve throughout the day.

Build a Wardrobe That Supports All Your Moods

Instead of asking “What is my style?”, try asking “What are my style modes?” Your wardrobe could have an Everyday Mode (Clean Minimalist), Creative Mode (Boho Artisanal), Off-Duty Mode (Street Cool), Romantic Mode (Soft Elegant), Night-Out Mode (Party Glam) and Power Mode (Formal Chic). Now your wardrobe isn't just a collection of clothes — it's a collection of possibilities.

How AHVI Uses Style Personas

title: Indian Wear Trends in 2026: What to Wear Now
excerpt: Sarees are being styled with contemporary silhouettes, kurtas are moving beyond ethnic sets, men are embracing jewellery — Indian wear is becoming more versatile, personal and wearable.
content:
Indian fashion is moving beyond the traditional-versus-modern conversation. In 2026, sarees are being styled with contemporary silhouettes, kurtas are moving beyond ethnic sets, men are embracing jewellery, and traditional crafts are finding their way into everyday wardrobes. The common thread? Indian wear is becoming more versatile, personal and wearable. Here are the trends to know — for both women and men.

1. The Modern Saree

The saree is getting a contemporary update. Pre-draped styles, statement blouses, belts, jackets and unexpected accessories are making it easier to take the saree from traditional occasions to dinners, parties and even modern work events.

  • Sculptural or corset-inspired blouses
  • Belts and contemporary drapes
  • Jackets over sarees
  • Minimal sarees with bold jewellery
  • Sarees with Western-inspired accessories

The same saree can look completely different depending on how you style it.

2. Statement Blouses

The blouse is becoming a styling piece in its own right. Halter necks, structured silhouettes, capes, high necks and interesting sleeves can completely transform a saree. A simple silk saree with a dramatic blouse can feel more contemporary without changing the saree itself.

One saree. Multiple personalities.

3. Indo-Western Is Everyday Style

Indian and Western pieces no longer need separate sections in your wardrobe.

  • Kurta + jeans
  • Saree + blazer
  • Lehenga skirt + shirt
  • Indian jacket + trousers
  • Chikankari + sneakers
  • Kurta + loafers

The goal isn't to make Indian clothing look Western. It's to make your whole wardrobe work together.

4. Lighter Lehengas

Lehengas are becoming easier to wear beyond the biggest celebrations. For wedding guests, festive occasions and destination weddings, look for lighter fabrics, subtler embellishment and separates that can be reworn. Think of the pieces individually: skirt + shirt, blouse + saree, dupatta + kurta.

A versatile lehenga can become several outfits instead of a one-event purchase.

5. Indian Co-Ords

Co-ordinated sets are an easy way to look put together. For women, this could mean a short kurta with wide-leg trousers, a printed set or a contemporary kurta-pant combination. For men, try relaxed kurta sets, matching trousers, or an Indian jacket with coordinated pants.

The real advantage? Break the set apart and suddenly you have more outfits.

6. Heritage Crafts, New Silhouettes

Traditional Indian craftsmanship continues to influence contemporary fashion. Chikankari, Banarasi, Kanjeevaram, Ikat, Kalamkari, Phulkari, Chanderi and block prints can all work beautifully with modern styling.

  • Banarasi + minimal blouse
  • Chikankari + trousers
  • Ikat + contemporary jacket
  • Block print + sneakers
The craft stays traditional. The styling doesn't have to.

7. Minimal Indian Dressing

Indian wear doesn't always need heavy embroidery or elaborate styling. Minimalism is having its own moment: ivory and neutral palettes, clean silhouettes, fine embroidery, simple silk, tonal dressing, one statement accessory.

A simple kurta with beautiful jewellery can make as much of a statement as a heavily embellished outfit.

Trends for Men

Indian menswear is becoming more expressive — particularly through silhouettes, layering and accessories.

8. Relaxed Indian Silhouettes

The traditional kurta is getting more relaxed — oversized kurtas, shorter lengths, wide trousers, relaxed pants and contemporary jackets, paired with sneakers for casual, loafers for polished, or traditional footwear for festive. This makes Indian wear much easier to integrate into everyday dressing.

9. Indian Jackets

Nehru jackets, bandhgala-inspired pieces and embroidered jackets are becoming versatile wardrobe layers — don't reserve them only for weddings. Try an Indian jacket with a plain T-shirt, shirt + trousers, denim, a simple kurta or tailored pants. One statement layer can completely change a basic outfit.

10. Men Are Wearing Jewellery

Jewellery is becoming an important part of men's styling too. Indian fashion has always had a strong jewellery tradition for men, and it's being reinterpreted in more contemporary ways.

  • Chains
  • Rings
  • Bracelets
  • Kada
  • Beaded necklaces
  • Brooches
  • Earrings
  • Watches

For a wedding, try a statement necklace or brooch. For everyday wear, a simple chain, bracelet or ring can be enough. The key is balance — you don't need to accessorise everything: kurta + watch + ring, bandhgala + brooch, T-shirt + chain. Small details can change the entire personality of an outfit.

11. Rich Colours, Softer Neutrals

Indian fashion will always have a love for colour, but modern styling is becoming more intentional. Rich shades such as burgundy, emerald, indigo, rust, plum and mustard work beautifully alongside ivory, beige, cream, black and soft pastels. Instead of wearing multiple statement colours, try building an outfit around one strong shade.

12. Occasion Is Part of the Outfit

Indian dressing changes depending on where you're going. A daytime wedding isn't a cocktail evening. A puja isn't a dinner. A summer celebration isn't a winter wedding. And your outfit needs to account for the weather too.

  • Daytime — lighter fabrics and softer styling
  • Evening — richer colours and statement accessories
  • Summer — breathable fabrics
  • Monsoon — practical footwear and lighter layers
  • Winter — jackets, shawls and layering

The best outfit isn't just beautiful. It works for the moment.

Use AHVI to Try the Trend Before You Buy It

Bring it to AHVI and ask “Can I recreate this with what I own?”, “Would this blouse work with my sarees?”, or “How can I style my kurta in a more contemporary way?” AHVI can work with your Indian and Western wardrobe, while considering your style, occasion and weather. title: Men's Fashion Trends for Fall 2026: What Men Are Wearing This Season
excerpt: Tailoring is back, but it isn't necessarily slim. Roomier trousers, heritage-inspired pieces and jewellery are shaping the modern approach: tailoring + casual, classic + unexpected.
content:
Men's fashion in Fall 2026 is getting more expressive. Tailoring is back, but it isn't necessarily slim. Trousers are getting roomier, layering is becoming more intentional, heritage-inspired pieces are returning, and accessories are doing more of the talking. There's also a noticeable shift away from dressing head-to-toe in one aesthetic.

The modern approach is: Tailoring + casual. Classic + unexpected. Minimal + statement. Old-school + modern.

Here are the men's fashion trends shaping Fall 2026.

1. Relaxed Tailoring

The suit isn't going anywhere — but the fit is changing. Instead of extremely slim tailoring, Fall 2026 is leaning toward roomier trousers, softer construction and relaxed proportions.

  • Wide-leg or relaxed trousers
  • Roomier blazers
  • Double-breasted jackets
  • Soft-shoulder tailoring
  • Longer jackets
  • Relaxed suit separates

You don't always need a matching suit. Try a blazer with jeans, tailored trousers with a knit, or a suit jacket with sneakers. The new tailoring is meant to move.

2. Wide-Leg Trousers

Skinny trousers are taking a back seat. Relaxed and wide-leg trousers are becoming one of the easiest ways to update a wardrobe.

  • Wide trousers + fitted T-shirt
  • Pleated trousers + knit polo
  • Relaxed trousers + oversized shirt
  • Wide-leg trousers + tailored blazer

The key is balance. If everything is oversized, the outfit can lose its shape — pair relaxed trousers with a more structured or fitted piece when you want definition.

3. The Return of the Proper Jacket

Fall is all about outerwear. This season, jackets are becoming actual style pieces, rather than something you throw on when it's cold.

  • Car coats
  • Harrington jackets
  • Suede jackets
  • Cropped jackets
  • Utility-inspired jackets
  • Leather jackets
  • Lightweight raincoats
  • Structured overshirts

Mid-length outerwear and heritage-inspired jackets are particularly relevant for Fall 2026. A great jacket can completely change a simple outfit — white T-shirt + trousers becomes white T-shirt + trousers + suede jacket, and suddenly feels like a different look.

4. Brown Is the New Everyday Neutral

Black, navy and grey will always have a place in menswear. But Fall 2026 is making room for richer earthy tones.

  • Chocolate brown
  • Espresso
  • Camel
  • Rust
  • Olive
  • Tobacco
  • Burgundy
  • Mustard

Chocolate brown is particularly prominent this season, appearing across coats, knitwear, trousers and accessories. Try a brown jacket + cream T-shirt + dark denim, chocolate trousers + navy knit, or simply brown shoes + neutral outfit.

5. Mustard Is Having a Moment

One unexpected colour making noise in Fall 2026 menswear is mustard yellow. It works particularly well as an accent against autumn neutrals like brown, green, navy and cream. You don't need a mustard suit — try a knit, scarf, shirt, cap, jacket or sweater. Think of it as a colour injection rather than a full commitment.

6. Heritage Style Gets Modern

Classic menswear references are coming back — but they're being styled differently.

  • Rugby shirts
  • Argyle knits
  • Plaid
  • Corduroy
  • Suede
  • Wool coats
  • Polo shirts
  • Loafers

The trick is not to make the entire outfit look vintage. Mix one heritage piece with something modern: argyle sweater + wide trousers, suede jacket + T-shirt + jeans, polo + tailored trousers + sneakers, wool coat + hoodie. Classic doesn't have to mean old-fashioned.

7. Layering Is the Outfit

Fall is the perfect season to actually build an outfit. Instead of T-shirt + jeans, try T-shirt + overshirt + jacket + trousers, or shirt + knit + coat, or T-shirt + cardigan + tailored trousers. Layering gives you more combinations without needing a larger wardrobe — and that's where a wardrobe full of individual pieces starts becoming a system.

8. Knitwear Gets More Interesting

Knitwear isn't just a winter basic anymore.

  • Knit polos
  • Textured sweaters
  • Cardigans
  • V-neck knits
  • Striped knits
  • Patterned sweaters
  • Fine-gauge layering pieces

A knit polo with relaxed trousers can replace a shirt. A cardigan can replace a jacket. A textured sweater can become the focal point of a simple outfit.

9. Sporty Pieces Meet Tailoring

Athletic clothing isn't disappearing — it is becoming more deliberate. The interesting combination is sportswear with polished pieces.

  • Track jacket + tailored trousers
  • Hoodie + wool coat
  • Sneakers + suit
  • Polo + pleated trousers
  • Technical jacket + classic trousers

The idea is contrast. One relaxed piece can make a formal outfit feel much more modern.

10. Suede Is Back

Suede is one of those materials that instantly makes an outfit feel more autumnal.

  • Suede jackets
  • Suede overshirts
  • Suede loafers
  • Suede boots
  • Suede bags

Brown and earthy suede works particularly well with denim, cream, olive and charcoal. A simple white T-shirt + jeans + brown suede jacket is enough to make the trend wearable.

11. Men's Jewellery Gets Bigger

Jewellery is becoming a much bigger part of men's fashion. Fall 2026 is seeing more attention on statement rings, chunky textured pieces, expressive brooches, beads and bangles.

  • Signet rings
  • Statement rings
  • Chains
  • Beaded necklaces
  • Bracelets
  • Bangles
  • Cuffs
  • Brooches
  • Earrings
  • Watches

You don't need to wear everything. Try T-shirt + jeans + watch + ring, blazer + chain, or knit + bracelet + watch. Jewellery is becoming another way for men to show personality.

12. Indian Menswear Goes Indo-Western

These global trends work particularly well with Indian wardrobes — kurta + wide trousers, kurta + straight jeans, Nehru jacket + T-shirt + trousers, bandhgala + relaxed trousers, Indian jacket + denim, kurta + sneakers + jewellery. You don't have to choose between Western and Indian fashion; your wardrobe can do both. (For the full breakdown of Indian menswear and jewellery pairings, see “Indian Wear Trends in 2026: What to Wear Now.”)

13. Shoes Are Getting Sleeker

Shoes are becoming an important way to balance relaxed clothing.

  • Loafers
  • Sleek sneakers
  • Chelsea boots
  • Leather derbies
  • Minimal trainers
  • Suede shoes

Wide trousers with sleek footwear create a cleaner silhouette. And sneakers don't have to mean casual — a clean pair can work with tailoring too.

14. The Statement Piece

Fall 2026 isn't about making every item loud. Instead, choose one thing that gets attention.

  • A great jacket
  • A colourful knit
  • A statement ring
  • A vintage watch
  • A bold shoe
  • A patterned shirt

title: What to Wear to Work Based on Your Profession: A Guide for Men & Women
excerpt: A lawyer walking into court has different requirements from a creative director heading to a studio. Here's what to wear to work, organised by profession.
content:
What you wear to work shouldn't just depend on the dress code. It should reflect what you do, where you work, who you meet and how you want to show up. A lawyer walking into court has different requirements from a creative director heading to a studio. A doctor needs practicality. A banker needs polish. A startup founder might have more freedom. A designer can experiment. And sometimes, the same person needs five different work outfits in one week — that's where understanding your professional style helps.

Here's what to wear to work based on your profession — for both men and women.

1. Corporate & Finance

Think banking, consulting, accounting, investment, corporate management and traditional offices. The goal is polished, professional and intentional.

Women: tailored trousers, structured blazers, pencil or midi skirts, button-down shirts, simple blouses, tailored dresses, loafers, pumps, structured handbags, minimal jewellery — blouse + tailored trousers + blazer + loafers.

Men: tailored trousers, formal shirts, blazers, full suits when required, Oxford shirts, loafers, derbies, minimal watches, leather belts — Oxford shirt + tailored trousers + loafers, or suit + dress shirt + polished shoes + watch for important meetings.

Style direction: structured, classic, refined.

2. Law

Legal environments often call for a more conservative approach, particularly for court appearances and formal client meetings.

Women: tailored suits, blazers, trousers, midi skirts, structured dresses, button-down shirts, closed-toe shoes, minimal jewellery. Men: dark suits, formal shirts, tailored trousers, blazers, Oxford shoes, loafers, simple watches, conservative ties when appropriate.

Style direction: sharp, professional, understated. The more formal the setting, the more important fit and grooming become.

3. Tech & Startups

This is where traditional workwear becomes much more relaxed — you can look professional without looking corporate.

Women: straight- or wide-leg trousers, jeans where appropriate, knits, relaxed shirts, blazers, midi dresses, clean sneakers, loafers, minimal jewellery. Men: clean T-shirts, polo shirts, Oxford shirts, chinos, straight-leg jeans, overshirts, lightweight jackets, sneakers, loafers — T-shirt + tailored trousers + clean sneakers, or Oxford shirt + jeans + loafers.

Style direction: smart casual, comfortable, modern.

4. Creative Industries

Think advertising, design, fashion, photography, film, media, music and creative agencies. Your clothes can communicate more personality here.

Women: statement jackets, interesting silhouettes, wide-leg trousers, vintage pieces, layered jewellery, printed dresses, statement shoes, denim, oversized shirts. Men: relaxed tailoring, statement shirts, overshirts, wide-leg trousers, vintage-inspired pieces, sneakers, loafers, rings, chains, interesting watches.

You don't need to dress dramatically — even one unexpected piece can make the outfit feel creative: black trousers + white shirt + statement jacket can be enough.

Style direction: expressive, individual, experimental.

5. Fashion & Beauty

If you work in fashion or beauty, your outfit can become part of your professional identity.

Women: trend-led silhouettes, statement accessories, interesting layering, monochrome looks, fashion-forward shoes, bold jewellery, structured bags, unexpected colour combinations. Men: contemporary tailoring, relaxed trousers, fashion sneakers, statement outerwear, jewellery, textured shirts, interesting accessories.

The key isn't wearing every trend. It's showing that you understand style.

Style direction: fashion-forward, personal, intentional.

6. Healthcare

For doctors, dentists, therapists and healthcare professionals, practicality matters. Your clothes need to look professional while allowing you to move comfortably.

Depending on workplace requirements — women: scrubs, trousers, simple tops, lab coats, comfortable closed shoes, minimal accessories, easy-care fabrics. Men: scrubs, polos, trousers, lab coats, comfortable shoes, simple watches. Avoid anything that interferes with movement or workplace hygiene requirements.

Style direction: clean, practical, professional.

7. Education

Teachers and professors need outfits that are professional but practical enough for a full day of movement.

Women: trousers, midi skirts, kurtas, shirts, cardigans, midi dresses, comfortable flats, loafers, simple jewellery. Men: Oxford shirts, polos, chinos, trousers, lightweight jackets, loafers, clean sneakers where appropriate. Indian workplaces can also make kurta + trousers an easy professional option.

Style direction: approachable, polished, comfortable.

8. Architecture & Design

Architects and designers often need clothes that balance creativity with practicality — you may be moving between studio, client meeting and site visit, so your outfit needs to adapt.

Women: wide-leg trousers, oversized shirts, structured jackets, comfortable sneakers, loafers, minimal jewellery, utility-inspired pieces. Men: relaxed trousers, overshirts, T-shirts, chore jackets, loafers, sneakers, utility-inspired layers. For site visits, always follow the required safety gear and footwear rules.

Style direction: functional, modern, design-conscious.

9. Hospitality & Events

Hotels, restaurants, event management and luxury hospitality often require a polished appearance with room for movement.

Women: tailored trousers, elegant dresses, blouses, skirts, loafers, low heels, minimal statement jewellery. Men: tailored trousers, dress shirts, polos, blazers, loafers, dress shoes. If your workplace has a uniform, use accessories and grooming where permitted to add personality.

Style direction: polished, welcoming, put-together.

10. Sales & Client-Facing Roles

When you're meeting clients, your clothing becomes part of your first impression — but the right outfit depends heavily on the industry. A luxury salesperson and a SaaS salesperson don't necessarily need the same wardrobe.

Women: tailored trousers, blazers, dresses, blouses, loafers, pumps, structured bags, elegant jewellery. Men: tailored trousers, shirts, blazers, chinos, loafers, derbies, watches.

The goal is to look credible without looking disconnected from the customer.

Style direction: professional, confident, adaptable.

11. Startups & Founders

There is usually more freedom — but that doesn't mean anything goes. Your wardrobe can become part of your personal brand.

Women: blazer + T-shirt + trousers, monochrome outfit + statement jewellery, shirt + jeans + loafers, minimal dress + sneakers. Men: T-shirt + tailored trousers + sneakers, Oxford shirt + jeans + loafers, knit polo + trousers, overshirt + T-shirt + jeans.

The goal is to look like yourself — but more intentional. Style direction: effortless, modern, personal.

12. Government & Traditional Offices

More traditional workplaces often have clearer expectations around professional dressing.

Women, depending on the workplace: sarees, kurtas, salwar suits, trousers, formal shirts, simple dresses, blazers, flats, loafers, minimal jewellery. Men: formal shirts, trousers, blazers, Nehru jackets for appropriate occasions, kurtas where culturally and professionally appropriate, loafers, formal shoes.

Indian wear can be incredibly professional — a well-fitted kurta + tailored trousers can look just as intentional as a Western business outfit.

13. Remote Work

Working from home doesn't mean you need to dress like you're going to a boardroom. But you still want to feel ready for the day.

Women: comfortable trousers, knit tops, shirts, simple dresses, coordinated sets, minimal jewellery. Men: polos, T-shirts, knit shirts, casual button-downs, chinos, comfortable trousers. And keep one reliable video-call outfit ready — you never know when “Can we jump on a quick call?” turns into an important meeting.

Style direction: comfortable, presentable, easy.

Your Profession Isn't Your Entire Style

Your profession tells you the context. Your personality determines the rest. Two lawyers can dress completely differently. Two founders can have completely different wardrobes. Two designers can have completely different aesthetics. That's because professional dressing isn't just “What is appropriate?” — it's also “What feels like me?”

Dress for the Day, Not Just the Job

Your profession is only one part of the equation. Your outfit should also consider where you're going, who you're meeting, the weather, your schedule, how formal the occasion is, and how you want to feel. You might have office → client meeting → dinner all in the same day.

Instead of changing your entire outfit, you can change the styling — add a blazer, swap sneakers for loafers, add jewellery, change your bag, add a jacket. Small changes can move an outfit from casual → professional → evening.

This Is Where AHVI Comes In

AHVI doesn't just ask “What clothes do you own?” — it can help answer “What do you need to wear today?” Tell AHVI: “I'm a lawyer and I have a client meeting today. Style me using my wardrobe,” “I'm a startup founder. Give me three smart-casual outfits for this week,” “I'm a creative director meeting a client. Make me look polished but not corporate,” or “I have a presentation at 10 and dinner afterwards. Create one outfit that can work for both.” AHVI can combine your profession, wardrobe, occasion, weather and personal style to create a look that actually fits your day.

Save the looks you love, reject the ones you don't. You don't need to pull everything out of your cupboard — make the mess on AHVI, then wear the winning look in real life. Your Work Wardrobe Should Work For You

You don't need a separate wardrobe for every version of yourself. You need pieces that can move between them. A blazer can work for client meeting → presentation → dinner. A kurta can work for office → festive event → dinner. A pair of trousers can work with shirt → T-shirt → knit → blazer. A good wardrobe gives you options — AHVI helps you discover them.

title: What Are All the Cool Girls Wearing in 2026?
excerpt: She somehow makes a simple outfit look expensive. The answer isn't one aesthetic — it's a mix of great basics, interesting proportions and a little bit of attitude.
content:
You know the girl. She somehow makes a simple outfit look expensive. She wears jeans differently. Her jewellery is always right. Her bag looks like she found it somewhere no one else knows about. And somehow, she never looks like she's trying too hard.

So what are all the cool girls actually wearing in 2026? The answer isn't one aesthetic. It's a mix of great basics, interesting proportions, vintage references, statement accessories, unexpected combinations and a little bit of attitude. Here's the cheat sheet.

1. The Perfect Pair of Jeans

Jeans are still doing the heavy lifting. But the silhouette is changing.

  • Straight-leg jeans
  • Relaxed denim
  • Wide-leg jeans
  • Dark denim
  • Vintage washes
  • Low-rise and mid-rise styles
  • Denim maxi skirts

The cool-girl trick? Don't make the jeans the entire outfit. Try relaxed jeans + fitted tank + oversized jacket, dark denim + crisp shirt + statement jewellery, or wide-leg jeans + tiny top + big bag. It's all about the proportions.

2. Tiny Top + Big Bottom

One of the easiest formulas for looking styled without looking overstyled.

  • Fitted tank + wide-leg jeans
  • Baby tee + oversized trousers
  • Cropped cardigan + baggy denim
  • Fitted knit + maxi skirt

The contrast creates the outfit.

3. Oversized Everything

The opposite works too — an oversized shirt, oversized blazer, oversized leather jacket, relaxed trousers. The trick is to let one oversized piece create the silhouette while keeping another part of the outfit more defined.

Oversized blazer + fitted tank + straight jeans is an easy starting point.

4. The Leather Jacket

The leather jacket continues to be one of those pieces that instantly changes an outfit.

  • Leather jacket + white T-shirt + jeans
  • Leather jacket + slip dress
  • Leather jacket + maxi skirt
  • Leather jacket + trousers

Don't overthink it. Throw it over almost anything.

5. Suede

If leather feels too obvious, go softer — suede is everywhere.

  • Suede jackets
  • Suede bags
  • Suede skirts
  • Suede boots
  • Suede belts

Brown suede is particularly easy to wear. White tank + jeans + brown suede jacket instantly feels more considered.

6. The Statement Bag

Cool girls aren't necessarily carrying the biggest designer logo. They're carrying interesting bags.

  • Vintage bags
  • Slouchy shoulder bags
  • Structured mini bags
  • Oversized totes
  • Unusual shapes
  • Colourful bags
  • East-West bags
  • Beaded bags

Sometimes the entire outfit can be: white T-shirt + jeans + incredible bag.

7. Jewellery Is Doing the Work

Minimal jewellery isn't the only option anymore. Layer it. Mix metals. Add something unexpected.

  • Gold hoops + rings
  • Silver chain + watch
  • Pearls + casual clothing
  • Stacked bracelets
  • Statement earrings
  • Chunky rings

The cool-girl approach is less about matching everything and more about making it feel collected.

8. Brooches Are Back

One of the easiest ways to make a basic outfit interesting? A brooch. Put one on a blazer, a coat, a cardigan, a scarf, a bag or a denim jacket. It gives even a simple outfit a vintage or editorial feel.

9. Ballet Flats + Unexpected Outfits

Ballet flats are having another moment. But don't style them in the most predictable way.

  • Ballet flats + baggy jeans
  • Ballet flats + tailored trousers
  • Ballet flats + leather jacket
  • Ballet flats + maxi skirt

The contrast makes them feel modern.

10. Loafers

Loafers aren't going anywhere — especially with wide trousers, mini skirts, straight-leg jeans and socks. The formula loafers + socks + trousers has become a cool-girl shortcut.

11. Sneakers With Everything

The right sneaker can make a dressed-up outfit feel effortless.

  • Dress + sneakers
  • Blazer + jeans + sneakers
  • Skirt + socks + sneakers
  • Tailored trousers + sneakers

The idea is to break up an otherwise polished outfit.

12. The Little Cardigan

A fitted cardigan is quietly becoming one of those wardrobe heroes. Wear it buttoned as a top, over a tank, with jeans, with a maxi skirt, over a dress, or under a jacket.

Cardigan + relaxed denim + ballet flats + shoulder bag. Simple. Very good.

13. Maxi Skirts

Mini isn't the only answer. Maxi skirts are giving cool girls another silhouette to play with.

  • Maxi skirt + fitted tank
  • Maxi skirt + oversized leather jacket
  • Maxi skirt + cropped knit
  • Maxi skirt + blazer

The long silhouette feels effortless and works across seasons.

14. The White Shirt

Still undefeated. But forget wearing it only with formal trousers.

  • White shirt + jeans
  • White shirt + maxi skirt
  • White shirt + mini skirt
  • White shirt + leather trousers
  • White shirt + denim shorts

Or wear it open over a tank. One great white shirt can do a lot of work.

15. Red

Red is the easiest way to make a neutral outfit feel intentional. You don't need a red dress — try a red bag, red shoes, red cardigan, red lipstick or red knit. Even one red accessory can become the focal point.

16. Brown Instead of Black

Black will always work. But brown is becoming the cool alternative — chocolate leather, espresso suede, brown boots, brown bags, chocolate trousers. Pair it with cream, denim, burgundy, olive or even pink.

17. The Feminine Dress + Tough Layer

One of the best styling tricks is contrast — take something soft, add something tough.

  • Slip dress + leather jacket
  • Floral dress + boots
  • Lace top + oversized blazer
  • Satin skirt + bomber
  • Feminine dress + chunky loafers

The contrast makes the outfit feel less predictable.

18. Sporty + Feminine

The cool-girl wardrobe isn't afraid of opposites.

  • Track jacket + maxi skirt
  • Sneakers + dress
  • Baseball cap + blazer
  • Sporty jacket + ballet flats
  • T-shirt + satin skirt

The unexpected combination is the point.

19. Vintage Pieces

Not everything needs to be new — vintage denim, old leather bags, retro sunglasses, vintage jewellery, thrifted jackets, grandma's brooch. A slightly imperfect piece can give an outfit more personality than something straight off a shelf.

20. Indian Pieces, Styled Differently

Cool-girl style isn't exclusively Western. Indian wardrobes have some of the best pieces for experimentation.

  • Saree + oversized blazer
  • Kurta + baggy jeans
  • Lehenga skirt + fitted tank
  • Silk saree + minimal jewellery
  • Indian jewellery + white shirt
  • Kurtis + sneakers
  • Traditional earrings + Western dress

The trick is to change the styling. Not necessarily the clothes.

21. The “I Just Threw This On” Outfit

The ultimate cool-girl aesthetic is looking like you didn't spend an hour getting dressed.

  • White tank + jeans + oversized jacket + sneakers
  • T-shirt + trousers + loafers + jewellery
  • Dress + leather jacket + boots

Simple pieces. Good proportions. One interesting detail. Done.

22. The Secret: It's the Combination

Here's the thing about cool-girl style. It isn't necessarily about owning rare clothes. It's about how you combine ordinary ones.

A white T-shirt isn't exciting. A white T-shirt with wide jeans + vintage belt + gold jewellery + suede bag suddenly is. A blazer isn't exciting. A blazer with tank + maxi skirt + sneakers feels completely different. The magic is in the styling.

Reject the looks you hate, save the ones you love, then get dressed. The experimentation happens on AHVI. The outfit happens in real life. The Cool-Girl Formula

You don't need all 22 trends. Start with great jeans, a good jacket, a fitted top, an oversized layer, one interesting bag, good shoes, jewellery, and one unexpected piece. Then learn how to combine them.

title: The Best Skirts for Your Body Shape
excerpt: Different silhouettes create different proportions, movement and visual balance. Here's how to choose between a midi, maxi, mini, A-line or pencil skirt for your shape.
content:
The right skirt can completely change the way an outfit feels. Not because there's one “perfect” skirt for your body — but because different silhouettes create different proportions, movement and visual balance. Your body shape can be a useful styling tool when choosing between a midi, maxi, mini, A-line or pencil skirt.

The five common shapes we'll look at are Pear, Hourglass, Apple, Inverted Triangle and Rectangle. And remember: body shape is about proportion, not size — you can have any body shape at any size. Let's find the skirts that work with your natural proportions, and more importantly, the ones you'll actually enjoy wearing.

1. Pear Shape

A pear shape typically has hips wider than the shoulders, a defined waist, and more visual volume through the lower body. The styling opportunity is to either highlight your waist or create balance between your shoulders and hips.

  • A-line skirts — one of the easiest choices; they gently skim the hips and create a clean line.
  • High-waisted skirts — highlight the waist and create a defined silhouette.
  • Flowy midi skirts — a fluid midi can look elegant without feeling restrictive.
  • Bias-cut skirts — the soft drape follows the body without creating a rigid shape.
  • Maxi skirts — especially beautiful when paired with a more fitted or structured top.

Try: high-waisted A-line midi + fitted top + cropped jacket, or flowy maxi + tucked-in shirt + statement earrings.

Styling tip: if you want more balance, add visual interest above the waist with statement sleeves, earrings, structured shoulders or brighter tops.

2. Hourglass Shape

An hourglass shape typically has shoulders and hips that are relatively balanced, a defined waist, and curves through the bust and hips. The easiest styling approach is often to let the waist remain visible.

  • Pencil skirts — a classic choice that follows the body's natural curves.
  • High-waisted midi skirts — they define the waist while creating an elegant silhouette.
  • Wrap skirts — adjustable and naturally waist-defining.
  • A-line skirts — great when you want something softer and more relaxed.
  • Bias-cut skirts — the drape can beautifully follow the body's natural lines.

Try: high-waisted pencil skirt + fitted knit, or wrap midi + tucked-in blouse + heels.

Styling tip: a tucked-in top, cropped jacket or defined waistband can help maintain the natural waistline. The important thing is definition, not tightness.

3. Apple Shape

An apple shape typically carries more visual volume around the midsection, with relatively slimmer legs and arms. The goal doesn't have to be “hiding” anything — instead, you can create a comfortable silhouette that lets the fabric skim rather than cling.

  • A-line skirts — they create movement away from the waist.
  • Flowy midi skirts — easy, comfortable and versatile.
  • Pleated skirts — soft pleats can add movement and create a longer visual line.
  • Wrap skirts — look for adjustable styles that sit comfortably rather than cutting tightly across the middle.
  • Straight midi skirts — a clean, uncomplicated silhouette can work beautifully.

Try: flowy midi + relaxed or half-tucked top + long layer, or A-line skirt + V-neck blouse + loafers.

Styling tip: high-rise doesn't automatically mean better — choose a waistband that feels comfortable and sits naturally on your body.

4. Inverted Triangle Shape

An inverted triangle shape typically has shoulders wider than the hips, a more defined upper body, and narrower hips and legs. This gives you an opportunity to add volume, movement or detail below the waist.

  • A-line skirts — a classic way to add gentle volume through the lower body.
  • Pleated skirts — pleats create movement and visual interest.
  • Full midi skirts — great for creating a fuller lower silhouette.
  • Tiered skirts — layers add volume and texture.
  • Printed skirts — a print can bring attention to the lower half of an outfit.

Try: pleated midi + fitted knit + simple shoes, or printed A-line skirt + minimal top + belt.

Styling tip: if you're looking for balance, keep the top relatively streamlined and let the skirt create the visual interest.

5. Rectangle Shape

A rectangle shape typically has shoulders and hips that are relatively similar in width, a less defined waist, and a straighter overall silhouette. This gives you plenty of room to experiment — you can create curves, emphasize the waist or lean into a clean straight silhouette.

  • Wrap skirts — they create definition around the waist.
  • Pleated skirts — they add movement and dimension.
  • A-line skirts — they create gentle shape through the hips.
  • Mini skirts — great for showing off the legs and creating a shorter, more playful silhouette.
  • Asymmetrical skirts — an unexpected hemline adds visual interest.
  • Maxi skirts with slits — they create movement and elongate the silhouette.

Try: wrap midi + fitted top + belt, or mini skirt + oversized blazer + boots.

Styling tip: belts, tucked-in tops and cropped jackets can all help create the appearance of a more defined waist if that's the look you're after.

The Skirt Length Guide

Your body shape isn't the only thing that matters — length changes the entire mood of a skirt.

  • Mini — playful, youthful and easy to dress up or down. Try oversized blazer + loafers, or fitted top + boots.
  • Midi — probably the most versatile length: work, brunch, dinner, weddings, everyday wear.
  • Maxi — elegant, dramatic and effortless. Try fitted top + maxi skirt + sandals, or knit + maxi + boots.

The Best Skirt for Your Style

Body shape is only one part of the equation — your personal style matters just as much. A pear-shaped woman might love a pencil skirt. An hourglass woman might prefer an oversized maxi. A rectangle-shaped woman might live in minis. There are no fashion rules you have to follow. Think of body shape as a styling tool, not a restriction.

How to Find Your Best Skirt Silhouette

If you're unsure where to start, try three different shapes — A-line, pencil and flowy/maxi. Take photos from the front and side, then ask yourself:

  • Which silhouette feels most comfortable?
  • Which one makes me feel most confident?
  • Which length works with my shoes?
  • Which one fits my lifestyle?
  • Which one works with the rest of my wardrobe?

The best skirt is the one that makes you want to wear it again.

Your Body Shape Is a Starting Point, Not a Rulebook

title: 4 Shoes That Work With Almost Everything: The Ultimate Shoe Capsule
excerpt: The right four pairs can take you from work to weekends, weddings to travel, jeans to dresses — without needing a different pair for every look.
content:
You can have a wardrobe full of clothes and still feel like you have nothing to wear. Sometimes, the problem isn't your clothes. It's your shoes. The right four pairs can take you from work to weekends, weddings to travel, jeans to dresses, and Indian wear to Western outfits — without needing a different pair for every look.

Here are the 4 shoes that can do the most work in your wardrobe.

1. White Sneakers

If you could only keep one casual shoe, make it a clean pair of white sneakers. They work with almost everything:

  • Jeans and trousers
  • Dresses and skirts
  • Shorts
  • Co-ords
  • Oversized shirts
  • Kurtas and Indo-Western outfits
  • Airport and travel looks

Try: white sneakers + straight-leg jeans + white shirt, or white sneakers + midi dress + denim jacket, or even white sneakers + kurta + straight trousers.

The key is to choose a simple silhouette that doesn't feel overly sporty. A clean, minimal sneaker will work with far more outfits.

2. Black Loafers

Loafers are the bridge between casual and polished — comfortable enough for everyday wear but structured enough to make an outfit feel intentional.

  • Tailored trousers
  • Jeans
  • Midi skirts
  • Dresses
  • Wide-leg pants
  • Blazers
  • Shirts
  • Indian-Western outfits

For women, try: black loafers + wide-leg trousers + fitted top. For men: black loafers + tailored trousers + Oxford shirt. And for an Indian-Western look: loafers + straight trousers + kurta or structured shirt.

They're especially useful when sneakers feel too casual but formal shoes feel like too much.

3. Minimal Sandals

A simple sandal is the warm-weather essential. Look for something minimal rather than heavily embellished — a pair that can disappear into the outfit rather than compete with it.

  • Dresses
  • Skirts
  • Linen trousers
  • Shorts
  • Jeans
  • Sarees
  • Kurtas
  • Co-ords
  • Holiday outfits

Try: minimal sandals + flowy midi dress, or minimal sandals + linen trousers + relaxed shirt, or minimal sandals + saree + simple jewellery.

They're perfect for summer, holidays, brunches, casual dinners and Indian occasions where you want something lighter.

4. Classic Ankle Boots

For cooler weather, ankle boots can completely change the wardrobe you already own.

  • Jeans
  • Trousers
  • Midi skirts
  • Mini skirts
  • Dresses
  • Leather jackets
  • Blazers
  • Sweaters
  • Coats

Try: ankle boots + straight jeans + oversized sweater, or ankle boots + midi skirt + fitted knit, or ankle boots + tailored trousers + blazer.

A simple black or brown pair will give you more versatility than a highly trend-driven boot.

The 4-Shoe Formula

  • White Sneakers — casual + everyday
  • Black Loafers — work + polished
  • Minimal Sandals — summer + relaxed
  • Ankle Boots — cool weather + elevated

Together, they cover a huge part of everyday dressing. And you don't necessarily need these exact colours — if your wardrobe is mostly cream, beige and brown, a brown loafer and brown boot may work better. If you live somewhere hot year-round, sandals may get more use than boots. If you dress mostly in Indian wear, you might swap ankle boots for juttis or Kolhapuris.

The best shoe capsule isn't about following a universal rule. It's about choosing the four pairs you'll actually wear.

How to Choose Your Four

Before buying another pair of shoes, look at what you already wear. Ask yourself:

  • What do I wear most often?
  • Do I dress more casually or formally?
  • Do I wear Indian, Western or both?
  • What's the weather like where I live?
  • Do I walk a lot?
  • What colours dominate my wardrobe?
  • What occasions do I dress for most?
  • Which shoes do I already own but barely wear?

Your lifestyle should determine your shoe capsule — not a trend list.

Make More Outfits With Fewer Shoes

Imagine you have 4 tops + 3 bottoms + 4 shoes — that's already 48 possible combinations before adding jackets, bags, jewellery or accessories. The goal isn't to own more. It's to make the things you already own work harder.

See the combinations. Save the ones you love. Then wear them in real life. (See “Make a Mess on AHVI, Not in Your Real Wardrobe” for the full idea.)
